title: Variables Primitive Types
subtitle: Java Teaching Studio · Live Session Lecture

title: Overview
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: A **variable** is the most fundamental building block of any Java program. Before you can write any meaningful logic, you must understand what variables are and how Java manages them.

title: Real-World Analogy
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: A **label** (the variable name) — so you can refer to it later.
A **type of content it can hold** (the data type) — a jar labelled *water* can only hold water; a jar labelled *coins* can only hold coins.
The **actual content** (the value) — e.g., the number `32`.

title: Syntax
subtitle: Conceptual Details
code: dataType variableName = value;

title: Example
subtitle: ### Line-by-Line Explanation
bullets:
| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `int` | Data type — tells Java the variable will hold whole (integer) numbers |
| `var` | Variable name — the label you use to refer to this container |
| `=` | Assignment operator — puts the value into the container |
| `32` | The value stored in the container |
| `;` | Semicolon — required at the end of every Java statement |
code: int var = 32;

title: Memory Representation
subtitle: When int var = 32; is executed:
bullets: Java allocates **4 bytes** of memory on the **stack** (for local variables) or **heap** (for instance variables inside objects).
The name `var` is a reference to that memory location.

subtitle: Section Introduction

title: Overview
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Java has two important type-related properties that distinguish it from dynamically typed languages like Python or JavaScript.

title: Static Typing
subtitle: In Java, you cannot write:
bullets: The compiler knows the type of every variable before the program runs. This allows the compiler to catch type errors early.
code: var = 10;  // ❌ ERROR — data type not specified

title: Strong Typing
subtitle: In Java, each primitive data type has strict limits:
bullets: `int` can hold values approximately from **−2.1 billion to +2.1 billion**.
You **cannot** store a value like `99999999999999` in an `int` without a compile-time error.

title: Interview Question
subtitle: Q: Is Java a statically typed language? Is Java a strongly typed language?
bullets: **Static**: All variable types must be declared at compile time.
**Strong**: Each type has a fixed range and implicit out-of-range assignments are not allowed.

title: Full Syntax
subtitle: Conceptual Details
code: dataType variableName = value;

title: Variations
subtitle: Conceptual Details
code:
int age;           // Declaration only (no value assigned yet)
int age = 25;      // Declaration + initialization
int a, b, c;       // Multiple variables of the same type in one line
int a = 1, b = 2;  // Multiple variables with initial values

title: Syntax Breakdown
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Element | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `dataType` | One of Java's 8 primitive types, or a reference type (class/interface/array) |
| `variableName` | A legal Java identifier following naming conventions |
| `=` | The assignment operator |
| `value` | A literal, expression, or result of a method call compatible with `dataType` |
| `;` | Statement terminator — mandatory in Java |

title: 6.1 `char`
subtitle: ### Overview
bullets: `char c1 = 'A';` — Declares a char and directly assigns the character `A`.
`char c2 = 65;` — The integer `65` is the ASCII code for `A`. Java internally stores `65` and displays `A` when printed.
`char c3 = 97;` — The integer `97` is the ASCII code for lowercase `a`.

title: 6.2 `byte`
subtitle: ### Overview
code:
byte variableName = 100;
byte variableName = -50;

title: 6.3 `short`
subtitle: ### Overview
bullets:
| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Size | 2 bytes (16 bits) |
| Range | −32,768 to 32,767 |
| Default value | `0` |
| Representation | Signed two's complement |
code:
short s = 200;
short s = -1000;

title: 6.4 `int`
subtitle: ### Overview
bullets:
| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Size | 4 bytes (32 bits) |
| Range | −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (approximately ±2.1 billion) |
| Default value | `0` |
| Representation | Signed two's complement |

title: 6.5 `long`
subtitle: ### Overview
bullets: Use `long` when your value exceeds the range of `int` (greater than ~2.1 billion). Common use cases include timestamps (milliseconds since epoch), large file sizes, and population counters.

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Size | 8 bytes (64 bits) |
| Range | −9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 (approximately ±9.2 × 10^18) |
| Default value | `0L` |
| Representation | Signed two's complement |
code:
long bigNumber = 500L;               // 'L' suffix tells Java this is a long literal
long worldPopulation = 8_000_000_000L;

title: 6.6 `float`
subtitle: ### Overview
bullets:
| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Size | 4 bytes (32 bits) |
| Precision | ~6–7 significant decimal digits |
| Default value | `0.0f` |
| Standard | IEEE 754 single precision |
code:
float price = 63.20f;   // 'f' suffix is REQUIRED
float pi = 3.14f;

title: 6.7 `double`
subtitle: ### Overview
bullets:
| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Size | 8 bytes (64 bits) |
| Precision | ~15–16 significant decimal digits |
| Default value | `0.0d` |
| Standard | IEEE 754 double precision |
code:
double price = 63.20;    // no suffix needed — double is the default
double price = 63.20d;   // 'd' suffix is optional but valid

title: 6.8 `boolean`
subtitle: ### Overview
bullets:
| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Size | Conceptually 1 bit (JVM implementation may vary) |
| Values | `true` or `false` only |
| Default value | `false` |
code:
boolean isLoggedIn = true;
boolean hasError = false;

title: Why This Matters
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: This is one of the most important (and confusing) concepts for beginners.
Java's integer types (`byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`) are all **signed two's complement** integers.
Understanding this explains why the ranges are asymmetric and what happens during overflow.

title: The Sign Bit
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: The **most significant bit (MSB)** — leftmost — is the **sign bit**.
code:
0 1 1 1 1 1 1 1  =  +127   (MSB = 0, so positive)
1 0 0 0 0 0 0 0  =  −128   (MSB = 1, so negative)

title: Why −128 to 127 (Not −127 to 127)?
subtitle: This gives 256 total values, and the range −128 to 127.

title: Overview
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Java frequently requires converting values between different data types. There are three kinds of conversions:

title: 8.2 Narrowing (Explicit / Downcasting)
subtitle: ### Definition
bullets: When you assign a value of a **larger** data type to a **smaller** data type, Java **does NOT** convert automatically.
You must explicitly tell Java to cast it.
code: smallerType varName = (smallerType) largerTypeValue;

title: 9.1 Member (Instance) Variables
subtitle: ### Definition
bullets: Variables declared **directly inside a class**, but **outside any method or constructor**. Each object (instance) of the class gets its **own private copy**.

| Property | Detail |
|----------|--------|
| Declared in | Class body (outside any method) |
| Default value | Yes (see Section 10) |
| Scope | Accessible from any method in the class |
| Lifetime | Lives as long as the object lives |
| Copies | One per object |

title: 9.2 Local Variables
subtitle: ### Definition
bullets: Variables declared **inside a method, constructor, or block**. They are created when the method is called and destroyed when the method returns.

| Property | Detail |
|----------|--------|
| Declared in | Inside a method or block `{ }` |
| Default value | **None** — must initialize before use |
| Scope | Only within the `{ }` block where declared |
| Lifetime | Exists only during the execution of that method |

title: 9.3 Static (Class) Variables
subtitle: ### Definition
bullets: Variables declared with the `static` keyword inside a class. There is only **one copy** for the entire class, shared by all objects.

| Property | Detail |
|----------|--------|
| Declared with | `static` keyword |
| Default value | Yes (same as member variables) |
| Scope | Class-wide |
| Lifetime | Entire program lifetime |
| Access | Via class name: `ClassName.variableName` |
| Copies | **One per class** (not per object) |

title: 9.4 Method Parameters
subtitle: ### Definition
bullets: Method parameters behave like **local variables** — they are created when the method is called and destroyed when it returns.
They have no default value — they are always provided by the caller.

title: 9.5 Constructor Parameters
subtitle: ### Definition
bullets: Variables listed in a **constructor's parameter list**. They receive values when a new object is created.

title: The Problem
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Both `float` and `double` follow the **IEEE 754** standard for floating-point arithmetic. This standard uses binary (base-2) representation for decimal numbers.
The problem is that many decimal fractions **cannot be represented exactly in binary**, just like `1/3` cannot be represented exactly in base-10 (`0.3333...`).
This leads to **tiny rounding errors** that accumulate during arithmetic operations.

title: Demonstration
bullets: We expected `0.2`, but got `0.20000002`. The same issue occurs with `double`.

title: Why Does This Happen? (IEEE 754)
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: The value `0.3` in binary is a **repeating fraction** (similar to `1/3` in decimal). The computer stores an approximation, and when you subtract another approximation, the tiny errors compound.

title: All 8 Primitive Data Types
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Type | Size | Range | Default | Use Case |
|------|------|-------|---------|----------|
| `byte` | 1 byte (8 bits) | −128 to 127 | `0` | Raw binary data, small integers |
| `short` | 2 bytes (16 bits) | −32,768 to 32,767 | `0` | Large arrays where memory matters |
| `int` | 4 bytes (32 bits) | −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 | `0` | General-purpose integer (most common) |
| `long` | 8 bytes (64 bits) | −9.2×10^18 to 9.2×10^18 | `0L` | Large numbers, timestamps |
| `float` | 4 bytes (32 bits) | ~±3.4×10^38 | `0.0f` | Approximate decimals (avoid for money) |
| `double` | 8 bytes (64 bits) | ~±1.8×10^308 | `0.0d` | Approximate decimals (avoid for money) |
| `char` | 2 bytes (16 bits) | 0 to 65,535 | `'\u0000'` | Single character |
| `boolean` | ~1 bit (JVM-dependent) | `true` / `false` | `false` | Logical flags, conditions |

title: Variable Kinds at a Glance
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Scope | Lifetime |
|------|-------------|----------------|-------|----------|
| Member (instance) | Class body | ✅ Yes | Whole class | Lifetime of object |
| Static (class) | Class body with `static` | ✅ Yes | Whole class | Whole program |
| Local | Inside method/block | ❌ No | That block only | Duration of method call |
| Method parameter | Method signature | ❌ No (caller provides) | Inside method | Duration of method call |
| Constructor parameter | Constructor signature | ❌ No (caller provides) | Inside constructor | During construction |

title: Type Conversion Summary
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
|
|------------|-----------|-------------|-----------------|
| Widening | Small → Large | ❌ Not needed | None |
| Narrowing | Large → Small | ✅ Required | Yes (possible overflow) |
| Promotion | During expression | ❌ Automatic | None (result in larger type) |

title: Most Frequently Asked Questions
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
**Q1: Is Java statically typed or dynamically typed?**
A: Java is **statically typed** — all variable types must be declared at compile time.

**Q2: Is Java strongly typed or weakly typed?**
A: Java is **strongly typed** — each data type has a defined range, and you cannot implicitly assign a value outside that range.

**Q3: How many primitive types does Java have? Name them.**
A: 8 — `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`.

**Q4: What is the default value of int, boolean, char?**
A: `int` → `0`, `boolean` → `false`, `char` → `'\u0000'`.

**Q5: Do local variables get default values?**
A: No. Only instance (member) and static variables get default values.
